Copper Long-term Outlook 

# Executive summary 

The big surprise for 2010 was that the strong start in global demand maintained its pace throughout the year and this resulted in double-digit growth in consumption, marking a stellar recovery from the contraction of 2009.  Demand has easily surpassed the level of 2008 but reassuringly, major regions in the developed world are maintaining the firm rate of recovery in the face of expectations of a slowdow

n.  Our overall estimate of demand growth in 2010 has remained in line with last quarter, while our 2011 forecast has been lifted, despite a softer growth rate in China.  Upgrades to Europe and North America outweigh the reduction in China.  Global refined copper demand rose by 10.5% in 2010, although this will expand at a slower rate of 5.0% this year to reach 20.2Mt.  Annual average refined consumption growth out to 2025 will be around 3.4%.  However, for now at least, the supply side response continues to lag this strength in demand, with refined production yet again set to expand at a slower pace than consumption, to increase by a modest 2.8% to 19.64Mt. This will mean that last year’s deficit is set to increase further, to just under ~600kt, driving prices higher still - we estimate that cash quotes will average $9787/t (4.44c/lb) in 2011. 

Overall base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 1.2% p.a. between 2010 and 2025 with output falling from a peak of ~19.6Mt in 2014 to ~13.7Mt in 2025.  For this year, demand for mine production will exceed available supply by the considerable margin of c.700kt and, ignoring highly probable and probable projects will largely be in balance for the following two years.  From 2014, the gap between demand for mine production and base case output will continue to grow, amounting to almost 38% of mine output by 2020.  However, when highly probable and probable mine projects are included (the latter being risked at 70% of production for brownfield and 50% for greenfield) in the medium term net additions to mine output are ~1.5Mt in 2012, ~1.3Mt in 2013, ~1.1Mt in 2014 and ~700kt in 2015.  The magnitude of this supply growth is such that the metal market is projected to be in significant surplus over the period 2013 to 2015.  Over the period to 2010 to 2025 we expect an additional 15.5Mt/a of mine project capacity to be commissioned.  This will be required to offset attrition and closures at existing mines (-2.6Mt/a) and to meet incremental demand. 

Our smelter production _capability_ forecast for 2011 now stands at 15.8Mt which is 7.5% higher than in 2010.  Last year, copper-in-concentrates contributed an estimated 85% (86% in 2009) of overall smelter output with the balance derived from scrap and purchased blister.  Average primary smelter capacity utilisation rates increased considerably in 2010 to 81.2% from 79.6% in 2009, although these rates remained well below the optimal industry level of 88%.  Overall, we expect an additional 9.8Mt/a of smelting capacity to be commissioned between the end of 2010 and 2025. 

The majority of revisions made to our smelter production capability forecasts are largely reflected in changes to our refinery output estimates.  Taking these into account, base case global copper refined production _capability_ is now expected to reach 20.6Mt/a in 2011 (+8%), 22.8Mt/a in 2012 (+10.5%) and 24.5Mt/a in 2013 (+7.4%).  However, base case refined production growth

is forecast to slow markedly from 2014 onwards and declining beyond 2017.  As a consequence, overall global capability will increase by only 1.4% p.a. between 2010 and 2025.  In tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~4.3Mt to 23.5Mt in 2025.  However, we expect an additional 9.8Mt/a of electro and fire refinery capacity to be commissioned over the period and a further 2.6Mt/a of SxEw production capability. 

Although 2010’s metal deficit was indeed small compared to the overall size of the market, its importance is more directly related to how this year will unfold.  We continue to believe the supply side will underperform again in 2011, leading to a deficit this year of more than four times that seen in 2010, of almost -600kt.  Refined production growth of just 2.8% will fall short of our projected demand growth of 5.0%, leaving metal stock days of consumption at well under 50 _vs._ last year’s 60 days.  Even into 2012 we currently show only a small surplus of ~85kt, which will keep stocks suppressed at 47 days.  Therefore, in the near term we expect prices to remain at elevated levels, averaging $9787/t ($4.44/lb) this year in constant 2010$, and edging down slightly as we progress through 2012 to $8771/t (US$3.98/lb).  The increasing contribution from new projects on refined production over the course of 2012 should remove some of the pressure from the market, pushing refined metal supply up by 7.8% to 21.2Mt, and so we would expect prices to reflect that towards the end of that year. 

As mentioned, by 2013 we are forecasting considerable supply-side increases to outweigh average demand growth projections, leaving the period through to 2015 showing structural market excess _averaging_ almost 1Mt/a metal.  Metal stocks, in terms of days of consumption, are projected to rise steadily, increasing from 60 days in 2013 to a peak of 84 days in 2015-2016.  A slight correction in 2017-2018 will bring a halt to that pattern, but even in 2019 we expect stocks to rise once again to 84 days.  Reflecting this, average prices are expected to fall to the cyclical low of $4189/t ($1.90c/lb) in constant 2010$ by 2019. 

Our long-term incentive price remains unchanged at $2.50/lb in current dollars over the period to 2025.  This has been derived from our analysis of mine project incentive prices and projected demand for mine production over this period, although we have made no allowance for potential mining-specific inflation which could further increase this forecast.

# Demand analysis 

## Overview 

**Copper demand builds momentum** The big surprise for last year was that the strong start to the year maintained its pace throughout 2010 to result in double-digit growth in global demand and marking a stellar recovery from the contraction of the prior year.  Demand has easily surpassed the level of 2008 but reassuringly, the major regions in the develo

ped world are maintaining the firm pace of recovery in the face of expectations of a slowdown as base effects work their way out of comparisons and normal seasonal patterns of consumption come back into play. Our overall estimate of growth in 2010 has remained in line with last quarter, while our 2011 forecast has been upgraded despite a softer growth rate in China. Upgrades to Europe and North America outweigh the reduction in China. Global demand rose by 10.5% in 2010, although will expand at a slower 5.0% this year to reach 20.2Mt. Annual average growth in demand out to 2025 will be around 3.4%. **Demand outlook for this year rests on Chinese shoulders** Heading into 2011 the big question mark over the outlook lies in China rather than in the more developed markets which have concerned interested parties the most over the past few years. The key question of the extent to which Chinese semis producers come back into the market and re-stock won’t be answered until the second quarter, which is the key period for our global demand forecast, and indeed, this will feed through into the sustainability of high prices also. At some point firms have to buy material as they simply need to fulfil their own orders but without a major re-stock at semis producers or if this is simply met by drawing down bonded warehouse stocks, then even our conservative Chinese forecast of 6% will be brought into question. However, this represents a downside risk to demand rather than our base case, which assumes re-stocking in the first part of the year and a solid upturn in refined imports into China. **Earthquake to have short term impact on economic activity** While the earthquake and subsequent tsunami represent a truly awful human tragedy, we do not anticipate a major impact on Japanese economic activity or demand. Without doubt, economic activity will be affected in the very short run, as much caused by logistical problems as damage to infrastructure and manufacturing capability but when looking at the Kobe earthquake the overall effects on the economy, while mildly positive, were more muted than might be imagined over the following years. ###### **Regional copper consumption – kt** ||||||||||**2025 vs 2010**

## China 

**China maintained double-digit growth in 2010** With most of the full year data now in, we estimate that Chinese demand for refined copper grew by 13% last year as continued strong economic growth underpinned the expansion.  In particular, infrastructure spending continues to form the major part of end use demand and although this will decline over the forecast period, its massive importance to current copper demand cannot be understated. 

**Chinese inflation comes off the boil but only to a simmer** The latest figures for inflation, although still at 4.9% y-o-y in February, at least suggested that price rises are stabilising, while core prices even slowed on the prior month. Arguably, the better news came in the shape of industrial production data, which revealed 14.1% growth in the first two months of the year, up from the 13.5% pace of December and suggesting that recent measures to tame inflation are not unduly crimping industrial and economic activity.  Meanwhile, new loans were also less than expected, underlining the impact that China’s tightening measures are having on the economy. 

**Semis production off to slow start in 2011** Activity at semis producers slowed in the final part of the year and ahead of the Lunar holiday at the start of 2011 and although data from the CNIA is not yet available, our indications are that output has got off to a slow start.  Certainly, bookings at semis producers have picked up in March from the low levels of February but the pace has been lower than would typically be the case at this time of year.  The slower than usual upturn

**First quarter re-stock disappoints** The same two factors are also impacting demand for refined metal, with semis producers keeping cathode stocks as low as possible in order to mitigate higher financing costs.  If you only have a certain amount of credit or working capital available for stocks, then the higher price of cathode means that you simply have to hold less metal in inventory.  This however, is against the seasonal norm, as there is typically a major re-stock through the supply chain in the first quarter of the year as firms build up stocks that were depleted in the final quarter. The accompanying chart reveals this pattern.  However, this year stocks are not building up in the supply chain but are mounting up in bonded warehouses instead. Although there is typically a major re-stock, the first quarter is the weakest in terms of underlying demand and semis production. It is not particularly surprising given the disruption from the New Year holiday period in addition to the cold weather in China at the time but there is also a seasonal aspect to many end-use markets such as for ACR tube. Given our expectations of a sharp quarter on quarter increase in semis output and refined demand in Q2, this material will need to be met either from bonded stocks or from imports. However, overall imports dropped sharply in February although at the time of writing the split between refined copper and copper products is not available and so we cannot be sure of the exact scale of the fall in refined imports, we do know they will have been sharply lower. **Construction to maintain solid if not spectacular pace** Infrastructure and construction spending are of key importance to Chinese copper demand although there are question marks over their performance this year as a result of government controls over real estate speculation in addition to a potential large stock of unsold housing. Starting with housing policy, tightening measures in Beijing have been introduced, requiring non-residents to provide five years of tax revenues in order to buy a house, and banning residents from buying a third home. Some estimates suggest that sales could fall by as much as 30% as a result of this. With other cities also introducing restrictions, Dragonomics estimates sales nationwide could dip 10% this year. Meanwhile, Chinese construction data has pointed to some possible alarming developments. Floor space under construction for 2010 totalled 27%, down from 29% in Jan-Nov, which suggests that year on year growth in floor space under construction fell below 5% in December. This cannot be explained by a rush of completions at the end of the year, as completions slowed even more sharply. For 2010, floor space completed grew by 5% but had been running at 10+% growth through the first 11 months. Floor space started, on the other hand, grew by 42% y-o-y in 2010. The data as a whole reinforces the idea that China potentially has a very large amount of property sitting near completion that is being held back from the market to avoid depressing prices. This clearly has direct implications for demand for the building wire segment as stocks of unsold properties will become an increasing drag on working capital and ultimately slow construction, especially given tightening credit conditions. A collapse in building remains a key risk to the economy in 2011, although the e

xpansion of low cost housing does perhaps provide something of an insurance policy for both the sector and the wider economy. Indeed, we forecast overall demand from the construction and infrastructure sector to rise in the order of 7-8% this year. While there is still plenty of scope for infrastructure spending in China in the medium term, the level of expansion will inevitably slow as China becomes a more developed economy and this will be reflected in a slower pace of growth from this sector in the latter part of our forecast period. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - March 2011 Page 6 of 32 Copper Long-term Outlook **AC production keeps the heat in demand** A further key component of demand will be from the consumer and general products sector, with air conditioner production providing the backbone of consumption. We estimate that copper used in air conditioners accounts for around half of this sector, with the balance made up with white goods and consumer electronics amongst others. Production of ACs has set off at a breakneck pace yet again this year while we are still to hit the peak period for demand which mirrors closely temperate patterns throughout the northern hemisphere seasons, with early summer being the peak period. As such, order levels are picking up strongly at tube makers and we expect solid growth in demand through this year. The medium term outlook also remains favourable given the large swathes of central and Western China that have yet to feel the level of development that Eastern China has experienced. Towards the end of the forecast period, however, the pace of growth from this sector will moderate as the growth of domestic purchasing slows and the level of global demand also eases. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - March 2011 Page 7 of 32 Copper Long-term Outlook ## North and South America **US economy improves, bringing up copper demand also** As the US economy grew stronger across all sectors during 2010, so did our confidence level of copper demand. Arguably, most of the damage to the copper sector was done during late-2008, when demand fell by 5.4% year on year, and throughout 2009, which saw a massive further drop of 18.5%. This left national demand at 2.4Mt, which was somewhat closer to levels of 30 years ago, and so it is no surprise that there was a recovery last year. Even so, the 6.1% estimated year-on-year improvement still left copper demand at a tepid 2.4Mt, which is some way off the 4Mt+ levels of a decade ago, and in this sense the word “recovery” must be used advisedly. **Copper rod output sets the pace…** Leading the way for this copper “recovery” was output of copper rod, which improved by almost 10% y-o-y to 1.26Mt. Apparent rod consumption increased by 5.9% last year, according to the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS), which was the first year of growth in four. But healthy domestic output was not the sole contribut

or to this statistic, as weaker imports (down 6.8%) combined with stronger exports (up by 27.8%) to tip the net trade balance in US rod producers’ favour. Despite the somewhat suppressed imports, Canada managed to increase its share to 91% last year to almost 95kt, largely from the Nexans rod mill in Montreal. Mexican rod made up the remainder, with zero imports coming from Russia in 2010 following 18.3kt imports in 2009. As in each year since 2005, 2010 continued with the typical pattern of stronger rod production in the first half vs. the second. Equally, the tail-off in the final quarter was heavier than expected. Domestic shipment rates followed suit, but year-end rod product stocks finished 3.2kt higher than at the start of the year. ###### **US copper wire rod production - (kt)** 30 550

**..and the semis sector shows some improvement** In contrast to the rod sector’s second half performance, other semis business showed some strength from the third quarter. Data to November from the ABMS suggest that apparent consumption of copper and alloy semis (incorporating rod/bars/sections, strip/sheet and tube) improved by almost 14% year on year to November at 1.02Mt (metric). The tube sector remains the critical drag on semis production and shipments, given the lacklustre construction market. Domestic shipments remained depressed, down by 3.7% at 256kt, but even here the market held up better than expected into the final quarter. **Improvement in copper consumption expected this year** We anticipate some further gains in US copper demand this year, albeit at a somewhat limited level of 2.5-3%. This is much improved, though, on the near 1% contraction in demand that we had pencilled in for 2011 in our last report, and this is due to the more positive economic environment. This stronger “starting point” has helped to reduce the declining profile for the duration of our forecast period 2011-2025, and we now project that US and Canadian demand for copper will decline by 1.8% p.a. and 1.2% p.a., respectively instead of the former 3.3% p.a. and 2.5% p.a. The contraction reflects ongoing structural changes in the global economy which will see manufacturing and semis capacity relocating to lower wage economies. Imports, rather than domestic production, will satisfy domestic copper demand. Therefore, while the region’s wire and cable markets will be supported by the upgrading of much of its other infrastructure, this will not necessarily result in increased production of North American copper wire rod. ## Europe 

**Europe makes strong start to the year** The European market for refined metal seems to be in rude health and is enjoying a firm start to 2011 after closing last year with an estimated 11% growth for the region overall representing some 3.96Mt of refined copper.  This is an upgrade on our previous estimate as the European manufacturing sector continued to perform well in the final part of the year in the face of mixed economic data. 

**Economic activity led by manufacturing** Euro zone industrial output slipped marginally in December, as severe winter weather impeded activity in Germany in particular.  On the same month a year ago, however, output was up by 8.2%, while fourth quarter growth was up by a solid 1.6% from Q3.  Industrial orders data suggests that the European recovery continues to be driven by manufacturing and indeed, this has translated into the cu

rrent steady growth in demand for copper.  Concerns about sovereign debt, although not completely dissipated, have receded for the time being and consumer confidence hit its highest level since 2007 in February. 

**Steady growth in demand this year** The solid momentum in industrial production and in manufacturing output in particular is supporting copper demand growth and will lead to 6.6% growth in European refined demand overall in 2011. The growth rate does come with a warning statement though as the pan European number is boosted by the exceptionally strong growth expected in Russia this year because of increased production of wire rod, while the abundance of scrap and expectations of a tight market mean that our total consumption growth rate will be ahead of our refined number. 

**Increased rod output to boost Russian refined demand** Russia’s first use copper consumption is expected to surge in 2011 after a change in the tax regime in December that will result in much of the cathode that was formerly exported staying at home for processing by domestic facilities.  The 10% tax on exports of cathode is not a new tax but a re-introduction following the cut in 2009, which resulted in a sharp reduction in wire rod output and increased exports of cathode.  However, it is important to note that some of the wire rod shipments that increased following the initial introduction of the tax on cathode exports were of a low quality and re-melted but with margins for rod production significantly lower than the 10% tax this was still an attractive option for Russian firms.  Our forecast for Russian copper demand now for 2011 stands at 600kt, compared to the estimated 435kt of refined copper consumed in 2010. 

Meanwhile, Aurubis has released its latest quarterly production data, which revealed a 14.5% year-on-year increase in wire rod output to 198kt in the October to December quarter of 2010, while cast shapes output was 8% higher on the prior year at 54kt.  For the full calendar year wire rod output was up by 24.4% on 2009 at 791kt, while cast shapes output surged by 39% to 214kt.  These figures do indeed represent very strong growth, although wire rod sales in particular are

For instance, Sweden’s Elektrokoppar recently revealed that they are cutting a production shift and in doing so reducing output of wire rod by around 20%. New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply. A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles. New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant extern

al to that purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. 

## Scrapping rates 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played

a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap. 

## Scrap consumption 

Copper produced from scrap (at smelters, refineries and in direct use) amounted to 4.56Mt in 2010, an increase of 10.4% on the prior year and accounting for 32% of copper consumed.  Direct use scrap took the lions share, representing some 58% of copper produced from scrap, with smelters (23%) and refineries (19%) producing copper from the balance. 

Scrap use posted a strong recovery in 2010, after contraction in the previous two years as declining copper prices resulted in a lack of incentive to collect scrap while sluggish industrial production meant limited scrap generation. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - March 2011 Page 29 of 32 Copper Long-term Outlook # Principle uses of copper Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products. Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated

55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use.  With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals.  This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable.  Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. 

In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products.  Of these, construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 33% of total copper consumption.  The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. 

Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for ai

r conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 33% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, owing to its high cost, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers.  In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried quicker along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have occurred within the home because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. times the capacity of Category 3 wire and are therefore more than capable of meeting the needs of today’s high-speed Internet services such as digital service links and cable modems.  High-speed digital service lines now provide computer data transmission 50 to 270 times faster than that of the fastest dial-up modem connected to a telephone line.  More importantly, with the number of homes connected to the Internet and usage continuing to increase strongly, demand for higher quality copper telecommunication wire and cable is expected to surge in the coming years. 

The other main wire and cable segment to supply the electrical sector is winding wire.  Winding wire demand accounts for an estimated 20% of copper wire rod consumption, making it the third largest wire and cable market.  Applications include transformers, generators, stereos, television sets and motors.  Indeed, it is the need to improve electrical efficiency of this last application, particularly in the mature economies, that has generated the most growth in winding wire demand recently.  This is because improved electrical efficiency involves using a larger conductor in order to reduce electrical resistance, as well as ensuring that the proper voltages are delivered when needed.  In addition, the efficiency of electric motors is being improved further by introducing copper into the rotor as opposed to aluminium.  Meanwhile, in the developing economies, demand growth will mainly stem from increased consumption of electrical goods as disposable incomes rise. 

Copper’s third largest consuming sector, industrial machinery and equipment, accounts for 13% of total consumption. Both copper wire and cable and semi products supply this sector which includes equipment and machinery, industrial valves and fittings, off-highway vehicles and heat exchangers.  Copper wire and copper and copper alloy products are also used in transportation equipment, copper’s fourth largest category.  This includes the automotive, marine and aircraft/aerospace sectors.  It is within the automotive sector that developments of new copper applications have been most concentrated in recent years.  Prior to 1930 copper and brass, having excellent pressure containing and anticorrosion characteristics, were the favoured materials to be used in brake tubing.  However, mass auto production in the 1940s led to the adoption of furnace-brazed steel tubing because it was much lower in cost.  Although this form of tubing is still widely used today, copper has re-gained some of its lost market share through the introduction of a copper-nickel alloy (90% copper/10% nickel) which is more resistant to corrosion from road mud and salt than steel piping.  Likewise, new technology has led to the development of a new brazed copper-brass automotive radiator which has the necessary requirements to recapture some of the market share displaced by aluminium over the past twenty years. 

Meanwhile, 42-volt systems, hybrid vehicles and nume

rous electrical and electronic applications provide additional growth prospects for the use of copper within the automotive sector Over the years the number of electrical and electronic components installed per unit has been rising steadily, thereby creating the need for growth in the power and signal distribution system (otherwise known as the wiring harness). Many of the electrical components will have to be redesigned in order to work effectively with the higher-voltage systems which could result in the copper content of some of the electrical components falling, but as more power becomes available, new electrical components will emerge. Such examples include electronic valve actuation and electric braking, resulting in several kilos of copper, per unit, being added. Forecasts have shown that over the next ten years, increases per vehicle will outweigh the decreases in copper required per component. Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products. Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 8% of total copper consumption. The three main end-uses are electrical appliances, military ordnance and coinage. The production of the new Euro coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products.
